rule: One entry per Phase A decision candidate, in the candidates registry's order, numbered D-19..D-61 (D-61 also fixes that numbering). Every entry is DECIDED — ratified by you on 2026-11-08 ('Ratify and freeze'), after the RV-54..RV-60 review pass — except the two candidates the merged Chapter 0 amendment 1 already closed, which are recorded as ACCEPTED_CH0_CORRECTION and are not Chapter 1 decisions. basis cites only Chapter 0 (plus amendment) ids; hea names techniques that show an approach works, never a basis. conformance names the tests that prove the disposition in this workspace.

ratified.scope: D-19..D-61 as reviewed (registries/review.json); the Git publication sequence remains separate authorizations

statuses.DECIDED: Ratified by you on 2026-11-08; implemented and proven executable before ratification.
statuses.ACCEPTED_CH0_CORRECTION: Closed by merged Chapter 0 amendment 1 (CORR-55, CORR-56); recorded for completeness.

decisions.question: Which objects get complete v1 schemas in Chapter 1?
decisions.recommendation: Complete v1 schemas for exactly the ten objects Phase A marked ch1_scope=required: obj-00, obj-02, obj-03 (both kinds), obj-04 with its four embedded parts (obj-05, obj-06, obj-07, obj-17), obj-18 and obj-32. Every other object gets, in Chapter 1: its classification (schema form, authority effect, hash form), its identity and canonicalization obligations, and a named owning runtime chapter that must write its full schema under Chapter 1's rules.

alternatives.option: Full schemas for all 42 types now, as HEA did for its v1 types
alternatives.why_not: Receipts and ledger rows depend on Chapter 2/6 semantics (ledger columns, outcome rules) that are not yet designed; schemas written now would be guesses that the runtime chapters would have to correct, breaking immutability-after-commitment.

decisions.compatibility: Deferred objects are constrained, not free: representation.json binds each to Chapter 1's rules, so later chapters add fields, never change the rules.
conformance: check: representation.coverage (42/42 classified, 10 required with schema files)

decisions.question: A tagged union, or a union fed by two subordinate schemas, for obj-03, obj-37 and obj-38?
basis: objects.json (one type, one minter per pair)
decisions.recommendation: One schema per object type with a required `kind` discriminator; kind-specific fields validated conditionally inside that one schema. The hash domain label is the record's kind (D-29), so the kinds can never collide in hashing even where their payload shapes coincide.

alternatives.option: Two subordinate schemas per pair with a thin union
alternatives.why_not: Implies two registries and invites the taxonomy split Chapter 0 deliberately avoided (RV-11).

decisions.compatibility: A future kind addition is a schema_version bump of the one type (D-39).

decisions.question: Where does a witness's admission live, and what does it hold?
decisions.recommendation: Admission is a section of the ExecutionReceipt (obj-15), as cap-30 already names it: `admitted_witnesses`, a set of entries {witness_kind, producer (PrincipalRef), content_sha256 (plain content address, D-31), admitted_utc, correlation facts (sequence_id, attempt_id, native ids as NFC strings)}. No new object type and no ledger row outside the 42 types, so no Chapter 0 correction. The entry's identity-bearing forms are fixed here; the full ExecutionReceipt schema stays Chapter 3's.

alternatives.option: A WitnessAdmissionRecord type of its own
alternatives.why_not: Chapter 0 has no such type among the 42; adding one needs a correction that cap-30 makes unnecessary.
Same correction cost, and it would detach admission from the receipt that INV-68/INV-69 classify.

decisions.compatibility: Chapter 3 adds diagnostics to the entry; it cannot remove the fixed fields.

decisions.question: Derivation, syntax, equality and lifecycle for each Autobot identifier.
decisions.recommendation: Typed, prefixed, lowercase identifiers with one grammar: `<prefix>_<32 lowercase hex>` where the 32 hex chars are 128 random bits minted by the owning seat, for: task_contract_id (tc, registry), sequence_id (sq, sequencer), attempt_id (at, sequencer), reservation_id (rv, sequencer), intent_id (in, sequencer), registration_id (rg, you via the authority service), delegation_id (dg, you via the authority service), duplicate_admission_id (da, registry), environment_id (ve, environment_probe), legacy_id (lg, migration). Name-form identifiers are operator- or author-chosen slugs matching `^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9._-]{0,63}$`: verifier_id, transform_id, repository_id, role names, assertion_id and edge_id (the last two unique within their contract). PrincipalRef is D-40's. Equality is exact byte equality everywhere; only the canonical lowercase spelling is valid; identifiers are immutable once minted, never reused, and no event changes one — supersession and revision mint new records that reference old identifiers. Full property sheets per identifier are in registries/identifiers.json.

alternatives.why_not: Conflates an identifier with an identity tier; INV-29 keeps tiers deterministic from their own inputs, and ledger rows are not records.
Encodes a timestamp into identity; R-6 orders authority by version and fence, never by time.

decisions.compatibility: Random 128-bit ids are collision-safe across machines without coordination.
conformance: test_identifiers: grammar, rejection of uppercase/short/foreign forms

decisions.question: What repository_id is, across clones and machines.
decisions.recommendation: repository_id is an operator-declared slug (D-22 name grammar, e.g. `autobot`), declared in the RepositoryAuthorityDeclaration you mint. The declaration is the authority that binds the slug to authority_location, canonical_ref and publication_mode; which clone, remote URL or machine realizes that repository is resolution-time context, excluded from every tier exactly like specification_inputs.resolution_path. Remote URL spellings (SSH vs HTTPS, user info) therefore never enter identity.

alternatives.why_not: Several spellings per repository, can carry credentials, breaks on renames and mirrors.
Forks share roots while having different authority; INV-26 wants your declaration to be the authority, not a content accident.

decisions.compatibility: A repository rename is a new declaration; old records keep citing the old slug and stay audit-valid.

decisions.question: Ranges, start values and overflow rules for the fence, versions and counters.
decisions.recommendation: Every number in a protocol object is an integer in [0, 2^53-1]; fractional numbers are forbidden outright, so the RFC 8785 number serialization reduces to exact decimal digits and every implementation agrees byte-for-byte. Start values: fence 1, Sequence version 1, revision 1, retry/repair counts 0, permitted/consumed/reserved uses 0, decomposition depth 0. Monotonicity scope: fence per Sequence, version per ledger row, revision per task_contract_id lineage. Reaching 2^53-1 is an integrity HALT, never a wrap. Policy structures fixed here: retry_policy {max_retries}, repair_policy {max_repairs}, reuse_policy {mode NEVER | FRESH_WITHIN, freshness_seconds when FRESH_WITHIN}, effect_policy {effect_intent_ttl_seconds, effect_hard_timeout_seconds} with hard_timeout < ttl (INV-67, SEM-12).

alternatives.why_not: RFC 8785 serializes numbers as IEEE-754 doubles; above 2^53-1 implementations diverge or lose precision, which is exactly the cross-implementation hazard D-09 exists to remove.

decisions.compatibility: 2^53-1 bounds every counter for any realistic lifetime; the HALT rule makes exhaustion visible instead of silent.
conformance: test_canonicalization: integer-only enforcement, 2^53-1 boundary, float rejection

decisions.question: The ordering rule for each collection field.
decisions.recommendation: Three collection shapes, fixed per field. A set is a JSON array sorted ascending by its member sort key, compared as UTF-16 code units (the same ordering JCS uses for object keys, so one ordering rule governs the whole spec); duplicate keys are rejected; a payload whose array is not in canonical order is rejected, never silently re-sorted. A map is a JSON object (JCS sorts keys; keys must be unique, NFC, and grammar-valid). An ordered list carries meaning in its order; no v1 identity field is an ordered list. Sort keys: allowed_scope.paths and artifact_paths by the path string; acceptance_assertions by assertion_id; finalization_requirements, capability_requirements, evidence_requirements by their enum/id string; predecessors by edge_id; resolved_bindings.verifier_registrations and transform_registrations by the digest text; mandatory_floor.mandatory_assertion_ids by the id; execution_requirements by the string; admitted_witnesses by content_sha256.

alternatives.why_not: What is hashed must be exactly what was given; silent transformation hides producer bugs and makes two byte-different payloads the same record (rejected-spelling principle, as for digests and NFC).

decisions.compatibility: Producers construct via the library, which sorts at build time; admission validates strictly.

decisions.question: Canonical paths and ref names, and the scope containment rule.
decisions.recommendation: A RepoPath is repository-relative: one or more non-empty segments joined by `/`, each segment NFC, containing no `/`, no NUL, no backslash, not `.` or `..`; no leading or trailing slash; case preserved and compared exactly. The single exception: the literal `.` is valid only inside allowed_scope.paths / allowed_scope.artifact_paths (delegation and contract scope sets), where it means the repository root and contains every path. Containment: P is inside S iff S is `.` or P == S or P starts with S + `/`; a contract's scope is inside a delegation's iff every contract entry is inside some delegation entry. A RefName is a full ref: `refs/` plus segments under the same segment rules, plus git's constraints (no `..`, no `@{`, no `.lock` segment suffix, no control chars, space, `~ ^ : ? * [ \`); comparison exact. No globbing in v1.

alternatives.why_not: Git object paths are case-sensitive; folding would merge distinct tree entries and make identity machine-dependent.
Containment becomes undecidable by inspection; prefix scopes are checkable and sufficient for INV-28.

decisions.compatibility: Backslash inputs are producer bugs surfaced at validation, not normalized away.

decisions.question: Format, precision and clock of audit instants, and the rule that they never order authority.
decisions.recommendation: Every protocol instant is the 24-character string `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS.mmmZ` (UTC, exactly millisecond precision, uppercase T and Z); any other spelling is rejected. The minting seat's system clock writes it: the authority service for authority records, the Registry for frozen_utc, the Sequencer for ledger instants, the probe for probed_utc. Normative rule, stated and tested: an audit instant never orders or gates authority — ordering is Sequence version, fence and CAS (R-6); the instants that end authority windows are D-28's and share only this format.

alternatives.why_not: Variable precision makes two spellings of one instant; fixed millisecond is one spelling and is what the coordinator's sources already produce.

decisions.compatibility: Fixed width survives lexicographic comparison for display; authority never depends on it.

decisions.question: Encoding of windows and how each window's end is computed and checked.
decisions.recommendation: Durations are non-negative integers in fields named *_seconds (D-24 domain), matching policy_defaults. Every authority window is persisted as an absolute end instant in a field named *_expires_utc (D-27 format), computed once when the window opens: end = the opening transition's instant plus the governing duration, under the effective bound (the stricter of policy and config, D-18). Expiry check: the window has ended iff now >= end (t-d02's comparison), evaluated by the Sequencer's clock for every ledger window and for delegation expiry; authority is valid strictly before the end. Reuse freshness: fresh_now iff now < acceptance instant + freshness_seconds. Observation windows (INV-31) use the same pair (duration in policy, absolute end in the receipt).

alternatives.option: Store only durations and recompute ends
alternatives.why_not: The end would depend on which event time a reader picks; persisting the end once makes every later check a single comparison against one recorded value.

decisions.compatibility: Windows never gain retroactive validity: a recorded end is immutable with its record.

decisions.question: Domain labels, framing, and which identities get labelled hashes.
decisions.recommendation: Every semantic identity hash is SHA-256 over domain_prefix || canonical_bytes. The domain prefix is the ASCII bytes `autobot/<category>/<name>/v1` terminated by one LF (0x0A); no prefix contains LF, so the framing is prefix-free and two different domains can never read the same input. Domains: `autobot/tier/requirement/v1` and `autobot/tier/contract/v1` for the two sub-tiers; `autobot/object/<kind>/v1` for every protocol object's object hash, where <kind> is the record's kind value (per-kind separation for multi-kind types, D-20) — obj-04's object hash is the record_hash and uses `autobot/object/TaskContractRecord/v1`; `autobot/closure/<kind>/v1` for artifact roots (D-32); `autobot/journal/transition/v1` for the journal chain. Content addresses carry no domain (D-31). Type and schema version bind through the domain, so tier preimages carry fields only.

alternatives.option: Type field inside the payload instead of a label
alternatives.why_not: Protects only payloads that remembered the field; the label protects every hash by construction and is checkable (SEM-17 ties payload.kind to the label).

alternatives.option: No domains (plain hash of canonical bytes)
alternatives.why_not: V-L: byte-identical payloads of different types would collide into one identity.

decisions.compatibility: New object kinds get new labels without touching existing ones; v2 constructions change the label's version segment.

decisions.question: How digests are written as text, and whether other spellings are rejected.
decisions.recommendation: Every digest-valued field is the 71-character string `sha256:` plus 64 lowercase hex digits. Uppercase, mixed case, bare hex, multihash or base64 spellings are rejected wherever a digest is read. Comparison is byte equality of the canonical text. This covers object hashes, tier digests, content addresses, artifact roots and journal hashes alike; whether a construction is domained (D-29) or plain (D-31) is independent of this one spelling.

alternatives.why_not: Not self-describing; a future algorithm change would be indistinguishable in stored data.

decisions.compatibility: Algorithm agility is explicit: a different algorithm is a different prefix under a new schema version.

decisions.question: Whether content-store addresses, specification input hashes and witness hashes are plain SHA-256 of exact bytes.
decisions.recommendation: Yes. A content address is the plain SHA-256 of the exact bytes, no domain prefix, written per D-30. This holds for content-store addresses, specification input hashes (INV-21's exact bytes) and admitted witness hashes (R-9's unchanged producer bytes). Semantic identities, which name meanings rather than byte payloads, are the domained hashes of D-29. The boundary is exact: if the thing being identified is a byte sequence, the hash is plain; if it is a typed object, the hash is domained.

alternatives.why_not: Breaks interoperability with standard tooling (sha256sum, git hashing pipelines) for no gain: byte payloads carry no type to confuse.

decisions.compatibility: Any tool can verify a content address against bytes with stock SHA-256.

decisions.question: How artifact_root is computed for each closure kind.
decisions.recommendation: artifact_root = SHA-256 with domain `autobot/closure/<kind>/v1` (D-29) over the canonical bytes of a ClosureManifest whose leaves are plain content addresses (D-31). Manifests: native {kind:'native', executable_sha256}; python {kind:'python', script_sha256, interpreter_id (an exact identity string such as 'cpython-3.12.4-windows-x86_64'), dependency_lock_sha256}; packaged {kind:'packaged', manifest_sha256} or {kind:'packaged', image_digest}. The manifest embeds exactly the closure contents Chapter 0 names for each kind; the domained root makes a native executable and a one-file python script with identical bytes distinct closures.

alternatives.option: native root = bare executable hash (no manifest)
alternatives.why_not: Two root constructions instead of one; and a bare content address as a root would collide with the executable's own address, blurring closure identity and content identity.

decisions.compatibility: New closure kinds add manifests without touching existing roots.

decisions.question: How Requirement, Contract and Record embed each other, and where the derived digests are placed.
decisions.recommendation: Digest-value embedding. requirement_digest = H(dom_req || JCS(requirement_preimage)) where the preimage is the record's shape restricted to exactly the nine requirement fields. contract_digest = H(dom_con || JCS({requirement_digest: <text>, …the sixteen contract fields})). record_hash = H(`autobot/object/TaskContractRecord/v1` || JCS({contract_digest: <text>, …the seven record fields})). Preimages are constructed at hashing time, never stored; the three digest values live beside the record (ledger columns, D-04), never inside the bytes they cover; the stored payload is the full record, from which all three recompute. A tier therefore changes exactly when one of its own fields or its embedded digest changes, which is the tier algebra every vector asserts.

alternatives.option: Field-embedding (each tier rehashes all lower fields)
alternatives.why_not: Loses the layering proof: a reader could not verify the contract tier without re-canonicalizing requirement fields, and digest equality would no longer witness tier equality.

decisions.compatibility: INV-29 holds by construction: no preimage contains a higher tier's input.
conformance: test_digests cascade property (lower change implies upper change)

decisions.question: Version syntax, exact matching, and telling malformed from unsupported.
decisions.recommendation: Every protocol object carries schema_version matching `^v[1-9][0-9]*$`; v1 readers accept exactly the constant `v1`. Recognition taxonomy, in order: a value not matching the grammar is MALFORMED_VERSION; matching but not `v1` is UNSUPPORTED_VERSION; `v1` is SUPPORTED and proceeds to validation. The two refusals are distinct outcomes with distinct error codes, so audit can tell corruption from evolution.

alternatives.why_not: Immutable-after-commitment objects never need compatible ranges; exact constants are the only thing exact matching can verify.

decisions.compatibility: Works with D-35: recognition is the gatekeeper compatibility policy builds on.

decisions.question: May newer software parse v1; do old objects stay readable; when is a parsed version authority-eligible; LEGACY_READ_ONLY vs authority-valid.
decisions.recommendation: Committed objects stay readable forever: every future reader must keep a conformant v1 reader (R-2 makes the bytes immutable, so this is a code obligation, cap-50). A reader may parse any recognizable version for audit through an explicit audit mode whose result is marked AUDIT_ONLY and can satisfy nothing. A parsed object is authority-eligible only when its version is SUPPORTED by the evaluating code and full canonical-form validation passes. LEGACY_READ_ONLY (obj-40, D-07) is a storage class, not a version state: a legacy item stays non-authoritative even if its bytes happen to parse, until re-verified under D-07.

alternatives.why_not: Rewriting committed bytes breaks every recorded hash; R-2 forbids it.

decisions.compatibility: This is the compatibility policy; it changes only by appended decision.

decisions.question: Whether Autobot-minted authority objects reject unknown fields.
decisions.recommendation: Yes, strictly: every Autobot-minted protocol object's schema is closed (additionalProperties false at every level), and validation rejects any unknown field with ERR_UNKNOWN_FIELD. Autobot mints these objects itself (R-4), so an unknown field is always a defect or an injection, never third-party evolution. Producer witnesses are the opposite trust model and are D-38's.

alternatives.why_not: An ignored field can change meaning for a future reader while being invisible to the hash-trusting current one.

decisions.compatibility: Field additions are schema_version bumps (D-34), never silent.

decisions.question: How an absent value is written: tagged variant, sentinel, or never absent.
decisions.recommendation: An absent value is the absence of the key: the field is omitted entirely from the payload and from every preimage. null is forbidden everywhere (ERR_NULL_FORBIDDEN); sentinel strings are forbidden; required fields are never absent. JCS then gives absence one canonical byte form (no key), which is deterministic and distinct from every present value. Paired-absence rules (a freeze you author has no delegation_contract, no mandatory_floor and no delegation_id, all three together; supersession_provenance absent only for a first record) are semantic rules with tests.

alternatives.why_not: Invents a second representation of what JSON already distinguishes, and bloats every preimage.
Two spellings of absence (null vs missing) is exactly the ambiguity canonicalization exists to remove.

decisions.compatibility: JSON absence survives every JCS implementation identically.

decisions.question: How producer witnesses are preserved and parsed so unknown fields survive and grant nothing.
decisions.recommendation: The producer's exact bytes are the witness: admitted as an unmodified content-addressed copy (D-31), never re-serialized, never normalized. Parsing for correlation uses a tolerant reader: unknown fields are preserved in the bytes and ignored for correlation, and can grant nothing because witnesses are evidence_only (R-7) — only the fields the admission entry (D-21) extracts ever reach a transition precondition. Admission never fails because of unknown fields; it fails only when required correlation facts are absent (that is INV-69's INCOMPLETE, not a parse error).

alternatives.why_not: AutoSwarm, Helios and the CLIs evolve their own formats (U-06); refusing their new fields would turn third-party evolution into evidence loss.

decisions.compatibility: The dual rule is exact: Autobot-minted objects strict (D-36), producer bytes tolerant-and-preserved.

decisions.question: Registered enumerations and how they grow.
decisions.recommendation: registries/enums.json is the single enum register. Wire spelling is UPPER_SNAKE for closed value sets: finalization_class {READ_ONLY, SOURCE_MODIFYING}; authority_location {LOCAL, REMOTE}; publication_mode {DIRECT_REF_CAS, MEDIATED}; remote_verification_mode {PRE_PUBLICATION_REMOTE_VERIFICATION, POST_PUBLICATION_OBSERVATION} with absence (D-37) meaning no remote check (the SRD/SL/RO case); eligibility {AUTOMATIC, HUMAN_REQUIRED}; effect_result {HAPPENED, EXPECTED_OLD_STALE}; effect_intent_state (the six of states.json); intent_class {attempt_scoped, staging_delete, workspace_sync} (amendment 1, lowercase as transitions.json spells them); closure_kind {native, python, packaged} (lowercase per registrations.json); assertion_mode {DETERMINISTIC, HUMAN_ATTESTED}; edge_kind {RECORD, CONTRACT, REQUIREMENT}; edge_observation_requirement {ACCEPTANCE, ACCEPTANCE_FRESH}; finalization_requirement {LOCAL_CANONICAL_COMMIT, SEQUENCE_REF_COMMIT, STAGING_PUBLICATION, REMOTE_VERIFICATION, CANONICAL_PUBLICATION, POST_PUBLICATION_OBSERVATION}; evidence_requirement {EXECUTION_LIFECYCLE, COMMAND_GOVERNANCE, SESSION_TRANSCRIPT, REMOTE_CHECK}; registration kinds, attestation kinds, supersession kinds as the object registries name them; version_recognition {SUPPORTED, UNSUPPORTED_VERSION, MALFORMED_VERSION}. completion outcome values are AutoSwarm's vocabulary — Chapter 0's U-06, still open — so completion_policies.success_outcomes is registered as an open vocabulary (non-empty NFC strings) pending U-06, the one deliberate non-closed set. An enum gains a value only through a schema_version bump of every object that carries it; value sets are frozen per version.

alternatives.why_not: V-A's bytes must be decided by a register, not convention; typos would mint new identities.

decisions.compatibility: Open-vocabulary fields are listed as such in the register, so closing them later (U-06) is an append.
conformance: check: enums.consistency (schema const/enum values all registered)

decisions.question: PrincipalRef syntax, equality, stable identity and canonical encoding.
decisions.recommendation: A PrincipalRef is the principal's registered id in Chapter 0's principals.json: grammar `^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,63}$`, equality exact, canonical encoding the bare id string (e.g. `you`, `registry`, `git_sequencer`). The register is the authority: validation of an authority record checks membership against it. Ids are never reused; a renamed seat is a new principal; retirement is recorded in the register, never by deleting the id.

alternatives.why_not: principals.json already carries kind; duplicating it into every record invites divergence from the register.

decisions.compatibility: New principals are register appends; existing records are untouched.

decisions.question: Does authored_by only name the principal, or does the record carry authentication proof; where does that evidence live; what binds the IPC peer and presence proof to the record?
decisions.recommendation: authored_by names the principal only (a PrincipalRef, D-40); the record carries no authentication proof. Authentication evidence lives in the authority service's protected ledger: when the service mints an authority record it appends, in the same ledger transaction, an authentication journal entry binding {the minted record's object hash, the PrincipalRef, the AuthorityAuthenticationProvider's factor result, the IPC peer identity}. The binding is therefore transactional co-commitment inside the one component D-01/D-02 already protect, not a field of the portable record. In the interim in-process topology the journal entry records the in-process caller; the target topology (Chapter 8) swaps in the real IPC peer and presence factor behind the same entry shape.

alternatives.option: Embed a signature or factor proof in the record
alternatives.why_not: The proof is environment-bound (an IPC peer, a presence check) and unverifiable outside the service; embedding it bloats identity with bytes no other party can check, while the service's ledger is already the trust root (D-02).

decisions.compatibility: Chapter 8 strengthens the provider without touching record schemas.

decisions.question: Blob bytes or working-tree bytes for specification inputs in a repository.
decisions.recommendation: Committed blob bytes, exactly as git stores them (git cat-file blob), with no checkout filters applied. Working-tree bytes are machine-dependent — core.autocrlf rewrote every Chapter 0 file to CRLF on this machine (gate 20261108-phasec-013) — so one commit would hash differently per platform, which is the opposite of INV-21. An input resolved from the filesystem (not under git) uses the raw file bytes read without transformation. The re-hash at dispatch and collection (INV-37) fetches by the same rule, so a filter change can never masquerade as an input change.

alternatives.why_not: Measured divergence on this machine; identity would depend on gitconfig.

decisions.compatibility: LF/CRLF variants are distinct inputs by construction (V-H), which is true and visible rather than hidden.

decisions.question: The schema language and the structural/semantic split.
decisions.recommendation: JSON Schema draft 2020-12 as the structural language, restricted to a closed authoring profile: type, properties, required, additionalProperties:false, enum, const, pattern, items, minItems/maxItems, minimum/maximum, patternProperties, propertyNames, oneOf, and local $defs/$ref only — no remote refs, no format reliance, no annotations with effect. The contract library implements exactly this profile (stdlib, D-59), so the schema files are both standard JSON Schema (readable by any tool) and executable here without dependencies. The split: schemas decide structure (shapes, grammars, closed objects, enums); the runtime model decides semantics (cross-field couplings, containment, digest consistency, derived sets). Every semantic rule has an id (SEM-xx) in registries/semantic_rules.json and a parity test proving the schema alone does not catch it, which documents each exception as the candidate requires.

alternatives.why_not: Unreadable by standard tooling; T-15/T-18 show parity testing works with a standard language.

alternatives.option: Full JSON Schema with a third-party validator
alternatives.why_not: Violates the dependency boundary (D-59) and imports a nondeterminism surface (format, vocabularies) the profile excludes.

decisions.compatibility: Any conformant 2020-12 validator accepts the files; the profile is a subset.
conformance: check: schemas.profile (files stay inside the profile)

decisions.question: What the delegation and floor fields hold, with and without a delegation.
decisions.recommendation: resolved_bindings.delegation_contract holds the bound DelegationContract record's object hash (D-29/D-30). resolved_bindings.mandatory_floor holds {delegation: that same object hash, mandatory_assertion_ids: the sorted ids the floor requires} — the floor resolved for this contract (K-4 becomes checkable: the two hashes must be equal). delegation_id (record tier) is a consistency-constrained copy of the bound record's own delegation_id field: validation rejects any payload where it differs or where exactly one of the pair is present. A freeze you author (D-11) omits all three (D-37 absence). The two-tier appearance is therefore: the ContractDigest binds the exact immutable authority record (fulfillment policy), while delegation_id is admission provenance whose value adds no degree of freedom. Consequence for V-Q: an object with delegation_id changed while the bound record stays the same is impossible by validation — the vector becomes an executable rejection with a mechanical impossibility argument (both inconsistent forms rejected; a property test varies the id and never passes).

alternatives.option: delegation_id as independent provenance (names a lineage, record names a version)
alternatives.why_not: Two ways to disagree with yourself inside one record; every disagreement is a defect with no legitimate reading, so the constraint should make it unrepresentable.

decisions.compatibility: K-5 resolves: delegation_id can never vary independently; V-P stays valid (new record, same delegation_id).

decisions.question: What supersession_provenance holds, with and without a predecessor.
decisions.recommendation: supersession_provenance is {supersedes_record: the superseded TaskContractRecord's record_hash, authorized_by: the SupersessionRecord's (obj-38) object hash}, both required when present; the field is absent (D-37) for a record with no predecessor. Validation enforces both-or-neither of its members and rejects an empty object.

alternatives.why_not: Loses the your-decision link (obj-38) that makes the supersession authoritative (D-06).

decisions.compatibility: First records and successors are byte-distinguishable without sentinels.

decisions.question: Normalization of identity-bearing text.
decisions.recommendation: Identity-bearing strings must already be canonical: valid Unicode, NFC-normalized, no NUL, no unpaired surrogates; the validator rejects non-NFC input (ERR_NOT_NFC) and never normalizes silently — what is hashed is exactly what was given, and only the canonical spelling is admissible. Names, ids, refs and paths additionally forbid all C0 controls and leading/trailing whitespace; the objective (prose) allows internal whitespace including LF but no other C0 controls and no leading/trailing whitespace. JCS's string escaping then yields one byte form per admitted string.

alternatives.why_not: Hashing transformed bytes makes the stored record differ from what the author signed off; the rejected-spelling principle (D-25, D-30) applies to text too.

decisions.compatibility: NFD producers fail loudly at validation instead of minting lookalike identities.
conformance: test_canonicalization NFC cases (NFD rejected; NFC golden)

decisions.question: How later objects reference a contract's embedded parts.
decisions.recommendation: Record hash plus a typed part selector: {record: the TaskContractRecord's record_hash, part_kind, part_id} where part_kind ∈ {ASSERTION, DEPENDENCY_EDGE, ENVIRONMENT_CONSTRAINT, ROLE_TRANSFORM} and part_id is the part's contract-scoped id: assertion_id for assertions and their environment constraints, edge_id for edges (added to obj-07's v1 schema for exactly this purpose), the role name for role transforms. Parts gain no hash of their own — the record hash pins the bytes, the selector names the part, and the pair is stable because the record is immutable.

alternatives.option: Record hash + canonical selector path (JSON pointer)
alternatives.why_not: Pointers break when a sibling is added in a later schema version; ids are stable names the author chose.
Creates 4 new identity constructions for things that are already inside a hashed identity (within_tiers).

decisions.compatibility: Chapter 4/5 receipt schemas reference parts with one mechanism.

decisions.question: How an imported LegacyRecord is identified and what provenance it carries.
decisions.recommendation: A LegacyRecord is identified by the plain content address of its imported source bytes (legacy_source_sha256, D-31), plus a minted legacy_id (D-22) as its ledger handle; it carries import provenance {imported_from_system (NFC string naming the producer system), original_identifiers (sorted set of the identifiers the source already carried, as strings), imported_utc, imported_by (PrincipalRef)}. It has no object hash: it is legacy_read_only, never a v1 protocol object, and re-verification under D-07 mints new v1 records that cite the legacy content address.

alternatives.option: Adopt the source's own identifier as identity
alternatives.why_not: Foreign identifiers have unknown uniqueness and lifecycle; the bytes are the one thing import can vouch for.

decisions.compatibility: v13/v13-rc/v14 proposals import without inventing retroactive v1 identities.

decisions.question: Whether to append U-44's correction to Chapter 0.
decisions.recommendation: Closed by merged amendment 1 (CORR-55): the staging_ref and workspace_sync machines, initiation rules t-g01 and t-w01 minting obj-25 with class-specific checks, INV-47 revised, INV-74/INV-75 added. Chapter 1 incorporates it representationally: intent_class {attempt_scoped, staging_delete, workspace_sync} is a registered enum; the EffectIntent row's Chapter 2 schema must carry effect and intent_class; the per-class check lists are carried in representation.json as the binding model for obj-25's standalone contexts (the former open:[U-44] rules now bind through t-g01/t-w01).
decisions.compatibility: No Phase A artifact is rewritten; the resolution is recorded forward.

decisions.question: Whether to append U-47's correction to Chapter 0.
decisions.recommendation: Closed by merged amendment 1 (CORR-56): t-i06 now carries retry_for (the four attempt-scoped effects), the initiation checks (delegation_active_at_intent, reservation_held, fence_matches, effect_intent_committed, intent_ttl_gt_hard_timeout) and the retry preconditions (retry_same_effect, retry_same_target, retry_same_expected_old, binds_superseded_intent); INV-73 governs. Chapter 1 incorporates it representationally: the retry intent's bindings include the superseded intent's intent_id (binds_superseded_intent), and retryable vs not_retryable effect sets are registered data.
decisions.compatibility: As D-49.

decisions.question: Does a push that didn't happen get a receipt, and with which bindings?
decisions.recommendation: No receipt object for a remote push whose outcome is ABSENT or UNKNOWN_OUTCOME. INV-43's 'externally visible push' is one that happened; the authoritative trace of a non-happened effect is the EffectIntent's terminal state plus the journaled transitions (obj-36), which Chapter 2 owns. The one local exception Chapter 0 already makes stays: t-s18 consumes a CommitReceipt recording EXPECTED_OLD_STALE with reservation_released (the RV-48 conditional context). obj-27 and obj-28 therefore exist only for HAPPENED, which keeps obj-28's delegation_state_at_ponr and reservation_consumed common bindings valid (it is always a PONR receipt), exactly as the Phase A inventory notes anticipated.

alternatives.why_not: Every transition consuming obj-27/obj-28 follows HAPPENED; a negative receipt would be a proof object nothing consumes, and its bindings would need outcome conditions (the RV-25 problem) for no consumer.

decisions.compatibility: Audit of non-events reads the journal, which replay already reproduces (INV-10).
conformance: representation check: no transition requires obj-27/obj-28 outside HAPPENED

decisions.question: Is eligibility derived from hashed fields or stored, and if stored, where?
decisions.recommendation: Derived, never stored: eligibility = HUMAN_REQUIRED iff any acceptance assertion's mode is HUMAN_ATTESTED, else AUTOMATIC. The assertion mode is a field of each assertion (requirement tier), so eligibility is a pure function of hashed inputs: two records with one RecordHash can never differ in it, INV-29 is untouched, and no identity.json change (hence no Chapter 0 correction) is needed. t-c02's eligibility_computed is computing this function at freeze; the library exposes it as derive_eligibility().

alternatives.why_not: Changes identity.json (a Chapter 0 correction) to store a derivable value — pure redundancy with a new disagreement mode.

decisions.compatibility: INV-32's HUMAN_REQUIRED gate reads the derivation.

decisions.question: What a ManualAttestation of an assertion binds, and which receipts bind the attestations behind an attested result.
decisions.recommendation: A ManualAttestation(ASSERTION) binds {the contract's record_hash, the assertion by part reference (D-47), the CandidateReceipt's object hash (obj-16), and the attempt identity} — it attests this assertion on this candidate in this attempt. The VerificationReceipt's per-assertion results each record their outcome source: BY_VERIFIER with the registration's object hash, or BY_ATTESTATION with the ManualAttestation's object hash, so the receipt that t-s10 consumes is the binding point; the AcceptanceReceipt then binds path_taken (ARCHITECTURE §13) and reaches the attestations through the VerificationReceipt it binds. Full schemas stay with Chapters 4/5; the binding fields' identity forms are fixed here.

alternatives.why_not: Duplicates what the bound VerificationReceipt already proves; two lists can disagree.

decisions.compatibility: READ_ONLY and source-modifying contracts share the shape; INV-38's before-COMMITTING timing is a transition rule, not a schema difference.

decisions.question: What repository_declaration_bound_and_matching checks beyond INV-45.
decisions.recommendation: 'Bound and matching' at freeze means all of: (1) the declaration resolves as the bound obj-02; (2) authority_location equal (INV-45); (3) repository_id equal (D-23); (4) for a contract whose finalization publishes the canonical ref (SOURCE_MODIFYING, any path), target_ref equal to the declaration's canonical_ref — K-10 closes in the strict direction, since Chapter 0 defines no non-canonical target flow; (5) remote_verification_mode consistent with the declaration: any mode present requires authority_location REMOTE; a REMOTE canonical publication in v1 requires publication_mode DIRECT_REF_CAS to proceed (INV-56), while a MEDIATED-bound contract may freeze and then waits at BLOCKED_UNSUPPORTED_FINALIZER (INV-64) — the freeze check is consistency, not v1 executability; (6) finalization fit per K-6/K-7 (SEM-05).

alternatives.why_not: Would admit contracts whose PONR ref Chapter 0 never defines a path for; strictness is reversible by appended decision, laxity is not.

decisions.compatibility: K-10 and V-M stop being pending: V-M's new declaration keeps the canonical ref, so it freezes.

decisions.question: How your budget grants (t-s13) and rejections (t-c06) are recorded.
decisions.recommendation: As journal entries, not new record types: every transition you trigger that neither requires nor mints a record (t-s13, t-c06) must journal, in its TransitionRecord (obj-36), a decision payload {decided_by: your PrincipalRef, decision_kind: BUDGET_GRANT | ADMISSION_REJECTION, subject (the sequence or admission), and the grant or rejection facts}. ARCHITECTURE §15 already journals every transition; this fixes that for these two the journal entry is the record of your decision, replayable under INV-10. No new object type, no Chapter 0 correction; the payload's full field list is Chapter 2's.

alternatives.why_not: A Chapter 0 correction to create a record nothing consumes; the journal already holds authoritative history.
Operational config is excluded from identity and replay; a decision would vanish from history.

decisions.compatibility: Budget grants become queryable history without changing the 42-type taxonomy.

decisions.question: What the probe captures for a Python verifier, and what a constraint may constrain.
decisions.recommendation: The probe (cap-33) captures, as obj-18's typed fields: interpreter {implementation, version, executable_sha256 (a content address of the binary, never its path)}; platform {os, os_version, architecture}; env_vars — only the variables the contract's constraints name, never the full environment (secrets stay out of receipts); tools — for each tool a constraint names: {version, executable_sha256}. A VerificationEnvironmentConstraint may constrain: interpreter implementation and exact version list, platform os/architecture lists, named tool presence with exact version lists, and named env var exact values. The split with U-18/D-57: what runs (script, interpreter identity, dependency lock) is the registration's closure; where it runs (platform, tools, env) is the probe's. A mismatch is a HALT-grade mismatch, not a failure (ARCHITECTURE §11).

alternatives.why_not: Environment blocks contain credentials; receipts are durable and shared.

decisions.compatibility: Constraint vocabulary can grow by schema version; the capture rule (only what is named) is fixed.

decisions.question: The execution closure for verifiers that depend on the claude, codex and Python toolchains.
decisions.recommendation: Pin what is pinnable, declare the rest, and let the architecture carry the consequence. A Python verifier's closure is exactly registrations.json's: script content address + interpreter_id + dependency lock content address (D-32 manifest). A claude/codex-dependent verifier pins the CLI executable's content address and exact version into a native or packaged closure, and declares the unpinnable externals — the model service, login, model id — as execution_requirements entries of the form `service:<name>`. Normative rule: a registration with any service:* requirement is nondeterministic and is ineligible to verify a DETERMINISTIC assertion (SEM-16); it can only feed proposals, which INV-06 already caps (an LLM proposes, never authorizes PASS). So the closure question for LLM toolchains dissolves: their unpinnable part never sits on the acceptance path.

alternatives.option: Hash CLI + model id as if deterministic
alternatives.why_not: The service behind the id changes; a pin that does not pin is worse than a declared nondeterminism.

decisions.compatibility: When a future offline model is truly pinnable (weights digest), it registers as packaged with no service:* entry and becomes eligible.

decisions.question: Which proof methods Chapter 1 adopts.
decisions.recommendation: All five: (1) a second, independent JCS implementation in the harness (harness/jcs2.py, written against RFC 8785 directly, importing nothing from the library) that must agree byte-for-byte on every fixture and on randomized property inputs; (2) frozen golden vectors — canonical bytes and digests generated once, committed, and re-verified on every run; (3) property tests with a fixed seed: key-order invariance, absence vs null, set-order rejection, domain separation, NFC rejection, integer bounds; (4) schema/runtime parity tests: every SEM rule has a fixture the schema passes and the validator rejects; (5) a cross-process test: a child process (fresh interpreter) recomputes every golden digest from the fixtures and must emit identical values, standing in for the Registry and the Sequencer recomputing independently.

alternatives.why_not: Goldens catch regressions, not shared misreadings of the RFC; the independent implementation and property tests cover those.

decisions.compatibility: The five oracles are the acceptance gate's evidence of determinism across implementations and process boundaries.

decisions.question: The contract package's dependency boundary.
decisions.recommendation: src/autobot_contract depends on the Python standard library only (json, hashlib, re, unicodedata, dataclasses, typing, pathlib for file loading of its own schema set) and on nothing else: no AutoSwarm, no Helios, no HDB, no Git execution, no network, no authority-service runtime, no storage engine, no agent APIs, no third-party packages. Enforced executably: a conformance test imports the package in a fresh subprocess and asserts every loaded autobot module's imports are inside the allowlist, and that no socket, subprocess or DB module was pulled in by the package itself.

alternatives.option: Allow a vetted JSON Schema dependency
alternatives.why_not: D-43's profile validator removes the need; one dependency is a supply-chain and determinism surface the contract layer must not have.

decisions.compatibility: The Registry, Sequencer and verifiers can all embed the library without inheriting runtime coupling.

decisions.question: Whether Chapter 1 handoffs record continuation and the previous handoff's SHA-256, verified by a tool.
decisions.recommendation: Yes: every Chapter 1 handoff carries predecessor {handoff, sha256} (the form ch01-phase-a.json already uses), and check_chapter1.py recomputes the predecessor hash against the repository's copy, verifies latest.json, and verifies this phase's own handoff hash and sidecar when frozen. The chain rule is now registered, not conventional.

alternatives.why_not: The chain is only as strong as its weakest unchecked link; a checker makes every link executable.

decisions.compatibility: Matches the three existing handoffs; nothing is rewritten.

decisions.question: How Chapter 1 numbers its decisions and corrections.
decisions.recommendation: Continue Chapter 0's global sequences: these decisions are D-19..D-61 (43, in the candidates registry's order); future corrections continue at CORR-57; unknowns already continue at U-19; vectors keep V-*/P-* ids. D-15 stays permanently unassigned and is recorded as such. One global namespace keeps every cross-chapter citation unambiguous.

alternatives.why_not: Every existing registry cites bare D-/CORR-/U- ids; two namespaces would make old citations ambiguous.

decisions.compatibility: This very registry is the first artifact of the rule.
conformance: check: decisions.ids (contiguous D-19..D-61, candidate order, D-15 never used)
